paragraphs: An image may come with object names without indicating which region each name describes. This paper learns from that incomplete supervision: training examples provide images and associated annotations, but neither region-to-word correspondences nor overall scene labels. The task is to recover useful relationships between visual content and language while learning to annotate images.

The proposed discriminative model explicitly represents a mapping between image regions and annotation terms. It also treats the overall scene category as hidden information. A new variant of the latent support vector machine framework learns with both kinds of unknown variables, allowing local object correspondences and broader scene information to participate in the model.

Experiments show that the model is effective compared with the tested baseline methods. The hidden scene representation also allows test images to be clustered. The contribution is a way to learn richer visual-textual relationships from image-level annotations, without requiring the training data to identify every object's location or supply scene categories.
neurips-2010-a-discriminative-latent-mod.tldr: A latent discriminative model learns image-region-to-word correspondences and hidden scene categories from images with unaligned object annotations.

paragraphs: Structured prediction models represent relationships among several output variables, making parameter learning demanding when graphical models contain cycles and many parameters. This paper develops an approximate learning framework and message-passing algorithms intended to make such large models practical. Its starting point connects conditional random fields with structured support vector machines.

The authors show that a soft-max form associated with the conditional random field objective smoothly approximates the structured SVM hinge loss. They then use Fenchel duality and a local entropy approximation to construct their learning procedure. The algorithm computes exact gradients for the approximate objective and has a convergence guarantee; those properties concern the approximated problem.

An image-denoising experiment demonstrates the approach. Earlier treatment of this task shared parameters across groups of interacting variables, whereas the proposed algorithm efficiently learns many parameters. The authors report prediction improvements of orders of magnitude in that experiment. The result illustrates the practical value of a tractable approximation that supports a much more extensively parameterized graphical model.
neurips-2010-a-primal-dual-message-passi.tldr: A convergent message-passing framework learns large graphical models by optimizing a structured-prediction approximation with exact gradients.

paragraphs: Evaluating a trained model can require purchasing new labels, especially when held-out training data are unavailable for privacy reasons or do not represent the test distribution. This paper asks how to estimate the model's F-measure as accurately as possible when only a fixed number of labels can be obtained. The objective is better evaluation of a given model.

The proposed active estimation procedure chooses which test instances to label through an instrumental sampling distribution. This gives the evaluator control over where the labeling budget is spent, instead of simply drawing instances according to their frequency in the test population. An analysis separates sources of estimation error and identifies a sampling distribution that minimizes estimator variance.

The paper also examines conditions under which active F-measure estimates are more accurate than estimates from ordinary test-distribution sampling. The benefit is therefore conditional, rather than a claim that selective sampling always improves evaluation. Its central contribution is a principled connection between instance selection, labeling cost, and the uncertainty of a performance estimate.
neurips-2010-active-estimation-of-f-meas.tldr: Active sampling can improve F-measure estimation under a fixed labeling budget by choosing instances to reduce estimator variance.

paragraphs: Heartbeat classification from electrocardiograms is difficult because recordings differ both between patients and within a patient. Classification tasks also vary, some heartbeat categories are much rarer than others, and obtaining patient-specific labels from cardiologists is costly. This paper addresses these interacting difficulties through active learning that adapts to both the patient and the classification task.

Active learning makes the choice of labeled training examples part of the learning process. In this application, that choice supports adaptation while reducing the amount of patient-specific training data needed. The approach directly targets a practical bottleneck: a model needs information about an individual patient, but expert annotation of that patient's recordings is expensive.

The authors evaluate the method on a benchmark database of ECG recordings annotated by cardiologists. On the two primary classification tasks recommended by the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation, it performs considerably better than the compared recent methods. It also uses over 90% less patient-specific training data than those methods, demonstrating both predictive and annotation-efficiency gains in that evaluation.
neurips-2010-active-learning-applied-to-.tldr: Patient- and task-adaptive active learning improves benchmark heartbeat classification while using over 90% less patient-specific training data than the compared methods.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to infer hidden dynamics in continuous-time stochastic models that are Gaussian when conditioned on an underlying Markov jump process. This setup combines Gaussian variation with a hidden process that changes through jumps, allowing the model to represent abrupt changes within dynamics that unfold continuously over time.

The authors first study jump-diffusion models in which the drift of a linear stochastic differential equation can change at arbitrary times. They derive partial differential equations describing exact inference and introduce a mean field approximation described as very efficient. This provides an approximate route to recovering the hidden dynamics alongside a mathematical description of exact inference.

A new lower bound on the free energy extends the approach to Gaussian processes with arbitrary covariance functions. That extension includes the non-Markovian RBF covariance, broadening the range of temporal dependence the method can accommodate beyond the initial jump-diffusion setting.

Results on simulated and real data show high accuracy in capturing latent dynamics. These findings support the approach’s potential usefulness across several real-data modelling tasks, while describing demonstrated performance rather than a guarantee for every application.
neurips-2010-approximate-inference-in-co.tldr: The paper introduces efficient approximate inference for continuous-time Gaussian models with hidden jumps and extends it to Gaussian processes with arbitrary covariance functions.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to an unknown function whose evaluations are expensive. Sequential methods choose one input, observe its result, and update their beliefs before choosing again. When multiple evaluations can run in parallel, this pattern leaves a scheduling problem: several inputs must be selected before any of their outcomes are available.

The paper proposes a batch-selection policy that builds on effective sequential policies. It uses Monte Carlo simulation to select a collection of inputs whose behavior closely matches what a sequential policy is expected to do. This transfers guidance from sequential decision rules into a setting where evaluations must be committed together.

Across six benchmarks, the proposed approach significantly outperforms two baselines. The authors also find that it can deliver large advantages over a leading sequential approach when performance is measured per unit time. That qualification matters: the reported benefit reflects the opportunity to evaluate inputs in parallel, and the method is designed to make productive use of that opportunity.
neurips-2010-batch-bayesian-optimization.tldr: Monte Carlo simulation turns effective sequential Bayesian optimization policies into batch choices that can improve performance per unit time.

paragraphs: Spontaneous brain activity contains reproducible patterns, but learning a full-brain probabilistic model from limited, noisy recordings is difficult. The number of relationships to estimate is large, and signals vary across both people and recording sessions. This paper asks whether information from a population can help build individual connectivity models that predict unseen data.

The authors describe each subject's functional connectivity through a multivariate Gaussian process. Their estimation strategy imposes a common graphical structure across the population, using that shared structure as a prior for subject-level models. This supplies a way to combine group information while still producing a model for each individual.

In fMRI experiments, models learned with the population prior generalize better to unseen data than models using the alternative regularization schemes tested. The estimated graphs also reveal known cognitive networks as integrated communities of functional connectivity. These findings connect predictive validation with an interpretable organization of brain activity, supporting the usefulness of shared population structure for individual estimation.
neurips-2010-brain-covariance-selection-.tldr: Sharing graphical structure across a population improves individual fMRI connectivity models' generalization and reveals communities corresponding to known cognitive networks.

paragraphs: Different similarity matrices can describe different relationships among the same data points. This paper studies how to learn a kernel matrix from several such inputs under general convex losses. Earlier algorithms often addressed only one similarity matrix or restricted the choice of loss, motivating methods that accommodate a broader combination of inputs and objectives.

The authors develop several iterative algorithms with convergence guarantees. Their main construction extends mirror descent to collections of positive semidefinite matrices. The resulting EMKL algorithm requires O(m² log n) iterations for m input matrices and an n-by-n learned kernel. Each iteration solves a multiple-kernel-learning problem and performs m eigen-decompositions of n-by-n matrices.

A faster variant, REKL, avoids those eigen-decompositions by imposing a restriction on the objective function. Another proposed alternative requires only an SVM solver. Experiments on a real protein dataset with multiple similarity matrices illustrate the algorithms' effectiveness. The paper thus offers several computational routes, with the faster restricted formulation trading some objective flexibility for cheaper iterations.
neurips-2010-efficient-algorithms-for-le.tldr: Provably convergent algorithms learn kernels from multiple similarity matrices under general convex losses, with restricted variants reducing computational work.

paragraphs: U-statistics summarize data through a function applied symmetrically to groups of observations. This paper develops empirical Bernstein inequalities for the case where that function, called the kernel, is bounded. Such inequalities connect uncertainty to variability estimated from the observed data, making variance information part of the statistical bound.

The new results use empirical estimates of either the kernel's variance or a conditional variance appearing in an existing Bernstein-type inequality. Their derivation applies the same non-empirical inequality twice. When the U-statistic has order one, the results reduce to existing empirical Bernstein inequalities, so the contribution extends that established setting to statistics built from groups of observations.

The authors discuss applications to learning ranking and scoring functions. For bipartite ranking, they provide an efficient sorting-based procedure for computing the required variance estimates. They also suggest potential uses in test-set bounds and empirical racing algorithms for online scoring-function learning. These latter uses are presented as possibilities supported by the inequalities, rather than demonstrated application results.
neurips-2010-empirical-bernstein-inequal.tldr: New variance-adaptive bounds for bounded U-statistics extend empirical Bernstein inequalities and support potential ranking and scoring applications.

paragraphs: Drawing samples from a very large Gaussian Markov random field can be computationally demanding. This paper presents an exact simulation technique with a local construction: independently inject noise into each Gaussian factor, then compute the mean or mode of the perturbed model. The resulting optimization calculation produces a sample from the original Gaussian model.

Combined with standard iterative solvers for symmetric positive definite systems, the technique yields an efficient algorithm with essentially linear time and memory requirements. This makes it suitable for extremely large probabilistic models. The same construction also provides an efficient unbiased estimator of marginal variances, allowing it to quantify uncertainty as well as generate data.

The method additionally supports certain non-Gaussian continuous models whose interaction potentials can be expressed as finite or infinite Gaussian mixtures. Introducing latent mixture assignments makes the continuous variables jointly Gaussian conditional on those assignments. A block Gibbs sampler can then alternate between sampling assignments and the continuous vector, using the proposed algorithm for the Gaussian step.
neurips-2010-gaussian-sampling-by-local-.tldr: Independent local noise followed by a Gaussian mean computation enables exact sampling and efficient uncertainty estimation in large Gaussian graphical models.

paragraphs: Charles Bonnet syndrome involves vivid, complex visual hallucinations in people primarily affected by eye disease, without other neurological pathology. This paper uses a Deep Boltzmann Machine to explore a possible account of those hallucinations. The model links the brain's ability to generate internal imagery with mechanisms that stabilize neuronal activity.

The account rests on two hypotheses. First, the visual cortex learns a generative or predictive model of sensory input. Second, homeostatic mechanisms maintain activity levels, potentially causing internally generated visual content to emerge when sensory input is lacking. The computational model brings these hypotheses together and reproduces a variety of qualitative findings associated with the syndrome.

The authors also modify the model to represent a possible role for acetylcholine in balancing feed-forward and feedback processing. These results offer a hypothetical mechanism through which reduced input and activity regulation could interact. They suggest that generative models may help explain cortical learning and perception, without establishing the proposed biological account as the confirmed cause of the syndrome.
neurips-2010-hallucinations-in-charles-b.tldr: A Deep Boltzmann Machine explores how learned visual imagery and activity-stabilizing mechanisms could produce hallucinations when sensory input is reduced.

paragraphs: A learned kernel matrix describes relationships among the data used to construct it, but prediction also requires handling new points. This paper develops a regularized framework for semi-supervised kernel learning and establishes an equivalence with learning a linear transformation. That equivalence explains how the learned matrix defines a kernel function that applies inductively to unseen data.

The connection also gives a constructive way to kernelize most existing Mahalanobis metric-learning formulations. To address large datasets, the authors modify the framework to limit the number of optimization parameters. They further develop a semi-supervised dimensionality-reduction method by choosing the trace norm as the regularizer within the same general framework.

Experiments show significant improvements in nearest-neighbor classification accuracy across several domains. The dimensionality-reduction method also substantially shrinks the feature space while maintaining competitive classification accuracy. Together, these results show how the theoretical matrix-to-function connection can support useful prediction and compact representations, with a parameter-limited formulation intended to make the approach more practical at scale.
neurips-2010-inductive-regularized-learn.tldr: A regularized kernel-learning framework connects learned matrices to functions for unseen data and supports effective semi-supervised dimensionality reduction.

paragraphs: Many vision problems require factoring a matrix even though some entries were never observed. They may also impose geometric requirements on the factors, such as orthonormality in orthographic structure from motion. This paper develops a formulation that handles missing observations and additional constraints within the same optimization problem.

The authors express matrix factorization as a low-rank semidefinite program and solve it using an efficient quasi-Newton implementation. The formulation supports large-scale problems while allowing constraints to be incorporated directly. That combination matters because a useful reconstruction must both fit the available measurements and respect the structure required by its application.

Empirical evaluations suggest that, under the conditions of matrix completion theory, the algorithm reaches the optimal solution and needs fewer observations than the compared state-of-the-art algorithms. This is experimental evidence under stated conditions, rather than an unconditional optimality guarantee. The paper also demonstrates effectiveness on affine and non-rigid structure from motion and photometric stereo, showing the formulation's usefulness across several vision tasks.
neurips-2010-large-scale-matrix-factoriz.tldr: A low-rank semidefinite formulation enables large matrix factorizations with missing data and directly incorporates application-specific constraints.

paragraphs: Cutting-plane methods can train linear support vector machines quickly in practice, raising the question of whether their theoretical convergence rates are overly pessimistic. An earlier analysis required O(1/ε²) iterations to obtain an ε-accurate solution, and a tighter analysis reduced this to O(1/ε). This paper investigates whether that latter rate can be improved further.

The authors construct counterexamples that disprove the conjectured improvement for the cutting-plane methods under consideration. Their examples apply both to linear SVM training with hinge loss and to support vector methods optimizing multivariate performance scores. The result places a worst-case limit on these methods despite their strong behavior on many practical problems.

The same optimization problems nevertheless admit a faster approach. By exploiting the structure of the objective, the authors devise an algorithm converging in O(1/√ε) iterations. The distinction is consequential: the lower bound concerns the cutting-plane method, while additional use of problem structure permits better iteration complexity for solving the underlying task.
neurips-2010-lower-bounds-on-rate-of-con.tldr: Counterexamples limit cutting-plane convergence improvements, while an algorithm exploiting objective structure achieves a faster O(1/√ε) iteration rate.

paragraphs: Brain-machine interfaces infer intended movement from biological signals under voluntary control. Because individual observations provide information over time, a decoder needs a model of how movement evolves. This paper develops that trajectory model using two ideas: the user may be choosing among a small set of likely targets, and the same movement may occur at different speeds.

The authors incorporate both ideas into a generative model. Candidate targets could be suggested by objects in the workspace or by the user's gaze, while time warping accommodates variation in movement speed. Approximate inference uses a mixture of extended Kalman filters, bringing multiple trajectory possibilities into the decoding procedure.

The resulting algorithm decodes arm movements dramatically better than a decoder using a trajectory model with linear dynamics in the reported comparison. The finding supports the value of representing plausible destinations and flexible timing when integrating biological signals. It shows that assumptions about intended movement can materially affect decoding quality, alongside the information carried by the observed signals.
neurips-2010-mixture-of-time-warped-traj.tldr: A trajectory model combining likely movement targets with variable speeds improves arm-movement decoding over the tested linear-dynamics model.

paragraphs: Features sometimes come with a meaningful hierarchy: individual features form the leaves of a tree, and internal nodes represent clusters. Tree-structured group Lasso uses this hierarchy to encourage structured sparsity, assigning a group penalty to every node. The hierarchy is predefined, and the optimization seeks a sparse solution that reflects those feature groupings.

Although this penalty captures useful structure, it makes the learning problem difficult to solve. The paper develops an efficient algorithm whose key step involves the Moreau-Yosida regularization associated with the grouped tree. The authors show that this component has an analytical solution, providing a direct way to handle a central part of the structured regularization.

A second contribution is an efficient procedure for determining the effective interval of the regularization parameter. Experiments on the AR and JAFFE face datasets demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution makes an existing hierarchical sparsity formulation easier to optimize, helping turn meaningful feature trees into a usable learning constraint.
neurips-2010-moreau-yosida-regularizatio.tldr: An analytical Moreau-Yosida solution and efficient parameter-interval procedure make tree-structured group Lasso more practical to optimize.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovering a sparse signal when there are far more candidate coefficients than observations. Measurements follow a linear model with Gaussian noise, and only a small number of true coefficients are nonzero. The proposed multi-stage Dantzig selector repeatedly refines its estimate to improve on the standard Dantzig selector's recovery guarantees.

Under a stated condition on the design matrix, the authors establish a high-probability error bound for every l_p norm with p at least one. Its leading term depends on s−N rather than s, where s counts nonzero coefficients and N counts coefficients above a noise-dependent threshold of order σ√log m. A smaller additive term remains in the bound.

The improvement therefore depends on how many signal entries are sufficiently large. When all nonzero entries exceed the relevant threshold, the method achieves the oracle solution with high probability. The authors also establish high-probability recovery of the same number of correct features under a milder condition than the standard selector requires. These are conditional theoretical guarantees tied to the signal and design assumptions.
neurips-2010-multi-stage-dantzig-selecto.tldr: Iterative Dantzig selection improves conditional sparse-recovery bounds according to how many true coefficients exceed a noise-dependent threshold.

paragraphs: Some decisions must be made before a noisy objective value is observed, while an observable external state changes the objective's shape. This paper studies that setting for convex stochastic optimization. Its central question is how previous observations can guide the current decision when those observations were collected under different states.

The authors estimate the joint distribution of states and outcomes nonparametrically, then use it to weight past observations. Those weights effectively group similar states, allowing observations relevant to the current state to form a convex, deterministic approximation of the objective. They propose both function-based and gradient-based optimization methods, along with kernel-based and Dirichlet-process-based weighting schemes.

The methods are tested on a synthetic multi-product newsvendor problem and an hour-ahead wind commitment problem. Results show that Dirichlet process weights can provide substantial benefits over kernel weights. More broadly, the experiments support using nonparametric estimates to obtain good decisions in otherwise intractable problems. The approach connects state-dependent statistical estimation directly to an optimization problem that can be solved.
neurips-2010-nonparametric-density-estim.tldr: Nonparametric weighting of observations from similar states creates tractable convex approximations for state-dependent stochastic optimization.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding which supervised learning problems can be learned online. Its approach is to define complexity measures suited to online learning and connect those measures to learnability. The goal is a general account of what makes a learning problem manageable in this setting, rather than an algorithm for a single application.

The proposed measures include online analogues of Rademacher complexity, covering numbers, and fat-shattering dimension from statistical learning theory. These provide different mathematical ways to describe the richness of a learning problem. The authors establish relationships among the measures and supply tools for bounding them, making the definitions usable in theoretical analyses.

The framework is applied to several learning problems and yields a complete characterization of online learnability in the supervised setting. This means the contribution goes beyond giving isolated sufficient conditions: it provides a characterization of when learning is possible within that setting. The relationships and bounding tools support applying that general result to particular problem classes.
neurips-2010-online-learning-random-aver.tldr: Online analogues of statistical complexity measures provide a complete characterization of supervised online learnability.

paragraphs: Matching people by body pose is difficult when clothing, backgrounds, and other appearance details change. This paper learns a nonlinear embedding intended to preserve pose-related similarity across those changes. The method extends Neighborhood Component Analysis and uses a convolutional design so it can operate on realistically sized images.

Training relies on inexpensive annotations of heads and hands in large video databases, collected through Amazon Mechanical Turk. The locations of these body parts act as a proxy for overall pose. This gives the method a concrete supervised task while allowing the learned representation to capture information beyond the individual points being labeled.

On challenging real-world data, the authors show that the method generalizes beyond hand localization to a broader notion of body pose. They also evaluate it quantitatively against other embedding methods and demonstrate that synthetic data can improve real-world performance. The findings support using limited body-part supervision to learn a more general pose-sensitive representation, with synthetic examples providing additional benefit in the reported setting.
neurips-2010-pose-sensitive-embedding-by.tldr: A convolutional nonlinear embedding uses head-and-hand supervision to learn broader body-pose similarity across appearance changes.

paragraphs: Learning a probabilistic automaton involves deciding both how it predicts sequences and what state structure it should have. This paper introduces a Bayesian nonparametric model with an infinite number of possible states, called a probabilistic deterministic infinite automaton. The authors also develop a sampler for inference in the model.

Given a finite training sequence, posterior prediction can be interpreted as averaging over multiple finite automata with different structures. Each candidate automaton is biased toward using few states. This allows structural uncertainty to enter prediction, and the authors suggest that averaging over automata offers a new approach to smoothing predictive distributions.

The model is tested on automaton structure learning and on prediction tasks involving natural language and DNA. Results suggest an attractive compromise between the computational cost of hidden Markov models and the storage requirements of hierarchically smoothed Markov models. The contribution therefore combines a flexible account of state structure with an empirically promising balance of prediction-related computational and storage demands.
neurips-2010-probabilistic-deterministic.tldr: A Bayesian infinite-state automaton predicts by averaging over compact finite automata with different structures.

paragraphs: Learning a latent-variable model can become trapped in a poor local optimum. This paper explores whether training examples can be introduced in an order that makes optimization easier. The motivating idea is to begin with easier examples and gradually include harder ones, but an appropriate measure of difficulty is often unavailable beforehand.

The proposed self-paced algorithm determines that ordering during training. Each iteration jointly selects easy samples and learns a new parameter vector. A weight controls how many examples are selected, and that weight is progressively adjusted until the full training set has been considered. Sample selection and parameter estimation therefore develop together.

Experiments compare the method with the state-of-the-art approach to learning a latent structural SVM across object localization, noun-phrase coreference, motif finding, and handwritten digit recognition. The self-paced method performs better in those four applications. These findings support adaptive example selection as a way to alleviate difficult optimization, without establishing that it always avoids poor local optima.
neurips-2010-self-paced-learning-for-lat.tldr: Self-paced learning jointly selects easier examples and updates model parameters, gradually expanding training to all samples.

paragraphs: Finding word boundaries in a phoneme sequence and learning what words refer to are closely related problems. This paper develops models that learn both at once: they divide phoneme strings into words while connecting some words to non-linguistic objects. The question is whether the two sources of information can improve each other's acquisition.

The models are Bayesian nonparametric extensions of Adaptor Grammars, built from an embedding of topic models into probabilistic context-free grammars. This provides a joint framework for segmentation and word-object relationships. The authors also model dependencies between words, allowing information about their relationships to influence both parts of learning.

Two findings support interaction between the tasks. Modeling inter-word dependencies improves both segmentation accuracy and word-object relationships. In addition, learning word-object relationships alongside segmentation produces more accurate segmentation than learning boundaries alone. The authors interpret these results as support for an interactive view of language acquisition, in which learning linguistic form and connections to the surrounding world can reinforce one another.
neurips-2010-synergies-in-learning-words.tldr: Joint models show that learning word boundaries, word dependencies, and object references can produce mutually beneficial improvements.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a classification loss controls the margin a classifier is encouraged to achieve. It analyzes relationships among the loss's shape, the optimal link function, the minimum risk, and margin enforcement. The purpose is to turn margin choice into an explicit design decision supported by mathematical relationships.

For a class called canonical risks, the authors show that asymptotic Bayes consistency is compatible with simple analytical relationships among these quantities. When the risk has canonical form and the link is inverse sigmoidal, a single parameter determines the loss's margin properties. They use this result to derive families of Bayes-consistent losses with adjustable margins.

Those losses lead to boosting-style algorithms that explicitly control the margin and generalize established methods such as LogitBoost. In experiments, the variable-margin losses outperform the fixed-margin alternatives used by existing algorithms. The authors also find that cross-validating the margin parameter can achieve the best performance. The results connect a theoretical loss-design framework to an empirically useful tuning choice.
neurips-2010-variable-margin-losses-for-.tldr: Bayes-consistent loss families make classification margins explicitly tunable and improve the tested boosting-style classifiers.

paragraphs: Topic models organize words through their associations with latent topics. This paper extends Latent Dirichlet Allocation by allowing additional information about words to influence the model's word distributions. The extension creates a way for resources such as dictionaries and thesauri to participate directly in topic learning.

The authors describe several capabilities enabled by this design. Side information can improve estimates for words that occur infrequently and encourage topics to be more cohesive within a language or across languages. In the multilingual setting, dictionary relationships bias corresponding words toward similar topics, providing a connection between vocabularies that the topic model can use.

Experiments focus on multilingual topic synchronization, using dictionary information to encourage this alignment. Results indicate substantially better topic cohesion than standard LDA. The stated evidence therefore supports the value of word-level side information for organizing multilingual topics. More generally, the approach makes external knowledge about words part of the probability model, rather than leaving topic structure to be determined solely from the modeled text.
neurips-2010-word-features-for-latent-di.tldr: Adding word-level side information to LDA improves topic cohesion, with dictionary-guided experiments demonstrating stronger multilingual topic alignment.
